Tracing the Impact of Payment Convenience on Deposits: Evidence from Depositor Activeness

August 2026

sections.name: Abstract (1/7)
sections.text:
How slow are bank transfers, and how do transfer delays affect deposit demand? Using transactionlevel data from millions of depositors, we measure transfer delays by matching debits and credits
across accounts held by the same depositor. Shorter delays correlate with more transfers and lower
balances. Exploiting county-level exposure to Zelle’s staggered rollout, we find that faster
payments reduce delays and deposit growth. Calibrating a deposit-management model, we find that
transfer delays raise deposit demand, and the magnitude of this effect varies with interest rates and
consumption volatility. Payment frictions therefore shape transactional deposit demand and
monetary transmission.
Xu Lu
University of Washington
Finance and Business Economics
xulu@uw.edu
Yang Song
University of Washington
songy18@uw.edu
Yao Zeng
University of Pennsylvania
The Wharton School
and NBER
yaozeng@wharton.upenn.edu
An Online Appendix is available at http://www.nber.org/data-appendix/w35638

1. Introduction Innovations in money and payments help facilitate economic activity (Brunnermeier, James, and Landau 2019, Duffie 2019, Parlour and Rajan 2025), and payment systems are increasingly central to banking and central banking design (Afonso, Duffie, Rigon, and Shin 2022, Copeland, Duffie, and Yang 2025, Correa, Du, and Liao 2025, Garratt, Yu, and Zhu 2025, Duffie 2026). Our paper demonstrates how payment technology shapes deposit demand. Using transaction-level bank data to measure payment delays, we provide direct evidence on how payment frictions affect depositors’ transactional demand for deposits. Our paper starts from a salient friction in the U.S. monetary system: deposits are the primary means of payment, yet many retail deposit transfers still take days to complete. We measure these delays and show that payment speed matters for how much depositors hold in transactional accounts. When transfers are faster, depositors move funds more actively across banks and maintain smaller transactional balances. Our account-level evidence further shows that balances in faster bank accounts are more responsive to outside rate incentives, consistent with depositors shifting funds more easily toward other banks or nonbank alternatives such as money market mutual funds, which we do not observe directly in the transaction data. Empirically, measuring depositor-level payment frictions is difficult because end-to-end payment times are not directly reported at a granular level. We propose a new measure of payment delays using transaction-level data from millions of depositors across depository institutions. We identify candidate transfer pairs by matching debits and credits across a depositor’s accounts using posting dates and transaction amounts, allowing an amount difference of up to $50. We then apply description-based and timing screens to infer likely interbank transfers. For each likely interbank transfer, we measure the elapsed time between the outgoing debit and the corresponding incoming credit, which we call the transfer delay . Using these matched transfers, we also construct a measure of depositor activeness, the deposit turnover: the gross flow of funds between a depositor’s accounts at different depository institutions. Transfer delays capture the payment frictions depositors face, while deposit turnover captures how actively they move funds across banks in response to payment frictions. We find that depositors facing longer measured transfer delays are less active in interbank 1

transfers and maintain larger transactional balances. These effects are stronger for depositors with higher consumption uncertainty and greater interest-rate dispersion across accounts, suggesting that depositors manage deposits to trade off liquidity for uncertain spending needs against the return to reallocating funds. Additionally, for a given depositor, accounts with faster payments have larger gross flows, especially among depositors with higher consumption volatility. The evidence suggests that payment delays dampen the sensitivity of retail deposit flows to rate incentives. A concern with the depositor-level evidence is selection: attentive depositors may choose faster accounts and also manage balances more actively. To complement the depositor-level evidence, we study county-level exposure to the staggered rollout of Zelle. We measure a county’s exposure using predetermined county-bank deposit shares and whether those banks subsequently adopted Zelle. This yields a reduced-form shift-share (Bartik) design in which counties are differentially exposed to the same payment technology rollout because of differences in their pre-existing banking composition. The key assumption is that, conditional on county and year fixed effects and controls, counties more exposed to Zelle-adopting banks would not otherwise have experienced different deposit growth trends. Following Borusyak, Hull, and Jaravel (2025), we show that banks more exposed to different types of counties were not systematically more likely to adopt Zelle earlier, and find that counties more exposed to Zelle adoption experience slower subsequent deposit growth. Greater Zelle exposure also predicts shorter measured transfer delays, providing an external validation of our delay measure. Taken together, the county-level results reinforce the depositor-level evidence that faster payments reduce deposit balances by making it easier for depositors to move funds. To interpret the evidence and quantify the deposit demand implications of faster payments, we develop a deposit management model with stochastic spending needs and random transfer delays. The model extends the Baumol-Tobin two-account framework by allowing depositors to hold a low-yield transactional account and a higher-yield savings account, while recognizing that transfers from savings to transactions do not arrive immediately. The innovation is to make payment delay a state variable in the household’s liquidity problem: after initiating a transfer, depositors face uncertainty about when funds will become available for spending. This generates a precautionary motive for holding transactional deposits even when they pay low interest. The model formalizes the trade-off suggested by the empirical evidence. Holding more transac- 2
tional deposits reduces the risk of being unable to meet spending needs while funds are in transit, but it lowers returns relative to higher-yielding alternatives. Shorter delays allow depositors to rely less on pre-positioned liquidity and move funds more frequently. The model generates the qualitative empirical pattern that faster transfers reduce transactional balances and increase turnover. We discipline the model using detrended moments and reduced-form estimates from our depositor-level data. The benchmark uses the sample-average interest-rate spread and a Pois- son completion intensity corresponding to a median completion time of approximately two business days. We use the estimated response of deposit balances to a one-business-day reduction in mea- sured delay to calibrate the proportional liquidity-shortfall cost, and use the benchmark transactional balance to determine the dollar scale of liquidity shocks. Finally, we use the calibrated model to conduct counterfactual analyses, evaluating the implica- tions of faster settlement. Increasing the completion intensity so that the median transfer-completion time falls from approximately two business days to approximately one business day lowers the modeled transactional balance by 21.8%. Under the calibration mapping that this balance represents 23.3% of total observed deposits, the exercise corresponds to a 5.1% decline in total deposit demand. The model also has implications for target balances, gross deposit reallocation, and state dependence across interest-rate and liquidity-uncertainty environments, with consequences for deposit stickiness, bank funding, and faster-payment design. Literature. Our paper first contributes to the line of work demonstrating how payments play a central role in banking and broader financial markets (see Parlour and Rajan 2025 for a survey). Prior research has shown that bank technology innovations influence borrowing and lending (e.g., Fuster, Plosser, Schnabl, and Vickery 2019, Berg, Burg, Gombovi ´ c, and Puri 2020, Parlour, Rajan, and Walden 2022), bank competition (e.g., Parlour, Rajan, and Zhu 2022, Sarkisyan 2023, Garratt, Yu, and Zhu 2025), international remittances and transactions (e.g., Du, Huang, and Scharfstein 2026), payment adoptions and choices (e.g., Chodorow-Reich, Gopinath, Mishra, and Narayanan 2020, Alvarez and Argente 2022, Crouzet, Gupta, and Mezzanotti 2023, Wang 2023), financial inclusion (e.g., Dubey and Purnanandam 2023, Higgins 2024), and risk-sharing for lower-income households (e.g., Jack and Suri 2014, Balyuk and Williams 2021). We add new evidence and a theoretical framework showing that faster payments allow depositors to maintain smaller transactional account balances, potentially increasing bank funding costs.
3
Our paper is closely related to an emerging literature that places payment systems at the center of banking and central banking design (see Duffie 2026, for a review). Earlier work shows that interbank reserve markets become stressed in periods of financial turmoil (Afonso, Kovner, and Schoar 2011), while recent evidence shows that balance sheet normalization increased intraday payment timing stress (Copeland, Duffie, and Yang 2025, Correa, Du, and Liao 2025) and that banks continue to economize on intraday liquidity even when aggregate reserves appear abundant (Afonso, Duffie, Rigon, and Shin 2022). Related work further estimates the reserve demand curve and measures reserve ampleness (Afonso, Giannone, La Spada, and Williams 2022, Lopez-Salido and Vissing-Jorgensen 2025, Lagos and Navarro 2026) and also models how payment timing affects money market rates (d’Avernas, Han, and Vandeweyer 2025) and how payment innovations affect demand for central bank reserves (Garratt, Yu, and Zhu 2025). We complement this literature by showing that payment delays at the retail level generate precautionary deposit demand and dampen depositors’ rate sensitivity, with implications for the quantity of reserves needed to support payments. Our paper also adds to the extensive literature on the demand for money and aggregate liquidity. An expanding body of research highlights convenience yield across various asset classes arising from factors such as liquidity, safety, and regulations (e.g., Stein 2012, Kacperczyk and Schnabl 2013, Sunderam 2015, Begenau 2020, Jiang, Krishnamurthy, and Lustig 2021, Acharya and Laarits 2023, Corell, Mota, and Papoutsi 2023, Brunnermeier, Merkel, and Sannikov 2024, Payne and Sz ˝ oke 2024). We show how transfer frictions create a convenience value for deposits and affect deposit demand and velocity. We further incorporate random payment delays and consumption volatility into a modern two-account money demand model in the style of Alvarez and Lippi (2009) and Kaplan and Violante (2014), presenting a novel addition to this longstanding theoretical framework since Baumol (1952) and Tobin (1956). Finally, with a focus on the payment role of deposits, our paper also contributes to the extensive literature on bank funding (e.g., Diamond and Dybvig 1983, Goldstein and Pauzner 2005, Drechsler, Savov, and Schnabl 2017, Egan, Hortaçsu, and Matvos 2017, Greenwood, Stein, Hanson, and Sunderam 2017, Whited, Wu, and Xiao 2022, Hanson et al. 2024), and specifically, to the burgeoning literature on the heterogeneous rate sensitivity of deposits and its implications (e.g., Acharya and Rajan 2024, Acharya, Chauhan, Rajan, and Steffen 2024, Chen, Goldstein, Huang, and Vashishtha 4
2024, Kundu, Muir, and Zhang 2024, Argyle et al. 2025, Cirelli and Olafsson 2025, d’Avernas et al. 2025, Egan et al. 2025, Benetton, Hebert, and McQuade 2026, Liu, Makarov, and Schoar 2026, Lu and Wu 2026). An emerging strand of research finds that deposits at digital banks are more volatile and serve more prominently as a medium of exchange (e.g., Erel, Liebersohn, Yannelis, and Earnest 2023, Koont 2023, Koont, Santos, and Zingales 2023, Cipriani, Eisenbach, and Kovner 2024, Jiang, Yu, and Zhang 2026). We show that more convenient payments encourage depositors to move funds more actively and maintain lower balances. We provide the first direct evidence of how payment speed and delays affect deposits, which carry important implications for bank funding, deposit franchise value, and financial stability more broadly. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 summarizes the datasets. Section 3 summarizes the motivating facts and measure of depositor activeness. Section 4 empirically tests how payment frictions affect depositor activeness and deposit balances. Section 5 develops a two-account deposit management model with transfer delays. Section 6 studies a counterfactual in which the median transfer-completion time falls from approximately two business days to one business day. Section 7 concludes.
2. Data Our empirical analysis combines several complementary datasets: (i) Transaction-level bank statements from a leading financial analytics firm track checking and savings accounts for 26 million U.S. depositors between 2014 and 2022, allowing us to observe individual-level fund movements across accounts and institutions. (ii) The FDIC Summary of Deposits (SOD) provides annual branch-level deposit balances for all FDIC-insured institutions, which we aggregate to the county level to construct measures of local deposit stocks and market concentration. (iii) We merge these data with county-level demographic and economic characteristics from the American Community Survey (ACS), including population, income, education, age composition, and measures of technology adoption, which are used as controls to account for cross-county heterogeneity and differential trends. (iv) Finally, we hand collect bank-level Zelle adoption dates by compiling historical snapshots of Zelle’s official partner-bank webpages from the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine.
5

2.1. Transaction-level data We use transaction-level, de-identified data on household spending, income, and transfers from a leading financial analytics firm. The dataset has been used in a growing number of studies in economics and finance (e.g., Baugh, Ben-David, Park, and Parker 2021, Blickle, Li, Lu, and Ma 2024). The database consolidates transaction data from more than 1,400 U.S. banks and credit unions, spanning American depositors with billions of transactions recorded from 2014 to 2022. The database includes savings accounts, checking accounts, credit, and debit card activities but excludes other account types such as brokerages and investments. In particular, deposits and withdrawals are observable for both savings and checking accounts. Transactions include information on dates, amounts, categories, and, when available, merchant names and locations. We use the textual description in the transaction data to extract information on depositors’ income, debt, spending, bank transfers, and monthly location through physical transactions. Following the recommendations of Baugh, Ben-David, Park, and Parker (2021) and Buda et al. (2022), we focus on the depositors who had at least ten spending, income, or transfer-related transactions each quarter. Because the sample does not include the entire universe of banks, this selection also helps to ensure that selected depositors primarily use bank accounts in the sample. Importantly, we note that the total deposit balance changes inferred from the data match the aggregate trends in the Flow of Funds (Figure 1) and we discuss the external validity concerns below in detail. We report summary statistics of depositors in the sample by the end of the section. External validity. Measuring payment delays requires us to focus on depositors with regular bank transactions. As a result, our sample is tilted toward individuals who actively use bank accounts for payments and may underrepresent cash-intensive or very-low-balance households. In addition, the transaction data do not cover every U.S. bank, so we retain depositors whose main accounts are held at participating institutions. While aggregate deposit growth in our sample closely tracks the Flow of Funds, the depositor-level relationships we estimate need not generalize to all households. We therefore interpret our results as applying to active retail depositors at U.S. banks and credit unions during 2014–2022, rather than to business, wholesale, or unbanked populations. Institution identifiers and empirical scope. The transaction-level provider supplies persistent depositor and account identifiers, which allow us to consolidate multiple accounts held by the 6
same person, but it does not supply a consistent institution identifier that can be used across all accounts and dates in the transaction panel, a limitation we return to in Section 3.3 when we describe how the two legs of a transfer are matched. Consequently, the depositor- and account-level specifications cannot include bank fixed effects or separately attribute realized delays to persistent
bank characteristics. At the same time, the transaction data offer information that is not available in standard bank-level datasets. The common depositor identifier allows us to link accounts held by the same person, match the outgoing and incoming legs of own-account transfers, and construct depositor-level measures of transfer delays and deposit turnover. We can then study how these measures vary with account use, liquidity needs, and interest-rate incentives. The SOD and Zelle data, in turn, contain bank identifiers, which we use in Section 4.3 to construct bank-level adoption shocks and county-level exposure. The absence of bank identifiers in the transaction panel therefore limits our ability to attribute delays to persistent bank characteristics, but not our ability to study depositor-level payment frictions or their responses to faster payment technology.
2.2. Other characteristics and constraints of depositors Account-level interest rates. We impute the interest rate for each bank account from interest income and the lagged account balance. Specifically, we compute interest income on deposits at the individual account level from credit transactions with a description containing the word “interest”. We manually filter out transactions that might misrepresent interest income such as transaction descriptions associated with bonuses, overdraft fees, loans, and rents. . One reason that depositors move money across accounts is that depositors shop for interest rates across bank accounts. We construct Rate Dispersion i,t as the difference between the highest and lowest rates offered across the bank accounts of depositor i in month t . This within-depositor spread is economically large relative to the level of rates: the average deposit rate in our sample is 9 basis points, while rate dispersion averages 13 basis points with a standard deviation of 25 basis points.
7
Expectation of overdraft. In our model, expected penalty costs serve as a key parameter prevent- ing deposits from turning negative. Although we cannot directly observe a depositor’s expectation of overdraft fees, we use two proxies. First, we consider whether a depositor has incurred any overdraft, non-sufficient funds, or returned check fees during the sample period. We track all transactions with descriptions related to these fees and create a dummy variable, Overdraft Realized i , which equals one if a depositor has paid such fees at least once. Second, a depositor’s decision to opt into overdraft protection services indicates their expectat

sections.text:
ion of overdraft fees. Banks often offer this service to help depositors avoid hefty fees. The service is often free if the accounts being protected and the funds being drawn are from the same bank, typically between a checking and a savings account, although some banks may charge a small fee, which is lower than the typical overdraft fee. We capture this by creating a dummy variable, Overdraft Protected i , which equals one if the depositor has a bank account with overdraft protection. Table 1 shows that 5% of depositors opt into overdraft protection services, while 21% have experienced overdrafts during the sample period, suggesting that many depositors anticipate liquidity shortfalls and the associated fees, which supports a precautionary motive for holding deposits. Salary. We construct salary income from credit transactions that are either categorized under ‘Salary/Regular Income’ or contain payroll-related terms in their description. We exclude any transactions related to social security, tax refunds, or UI benefits and consider both the transaction category name and specific keywords in the transaction descriptions. We validate the aggregate trend with labor income dynamics of depositors in our dataset against the corresponding dynamics in the PSID. Consumption volatility and stability. We use two measures to capture differences in consumption risk across depositors. First, we define Consumption Volatility as the 12-month rolling standard deviation of monthly consumption. Second, we construct a measure of Consumption Smoothing Efficiency (CSE), defined as the ratio of the 12-month rolling mean of consumption to its rolling standard deviation. This measure captures the stability of consumption relative to its level: a higher CSE corresponds to more stable consumption for a given average level of spending. These measures allow us to examine whether depositors facing greater consumption uncertainty respond differently to payment frictions and interest-rate incentives.
8
In addition, we compute each depositor’s residence at the state-city level based on locations they frequent and transactions containing location information, for example, restaurants, gas stations, utility bills, and groceries. In our analysis below, we find similar results with either depositor fixed effects or location fixed effects. Financial sophistication. We proxy for financial sophistication using the Digital Payment Ratio , defined as the share of a depositor’s total spending conducted online. A higher ratio indicates greater use of digital payment channels and, more broadly, greater familiarity with digital financial services. Table 1 provides summary statistics for depositors with active interbank transfers, highlighting substantial variability in deposit turnover, with an average deposit turnover of around $1,488.32 and a standard deviation of $968.10. We defer the formal construction of transfer delays and deposit turnover to Section 3. Dollar-weighted transfer delays vary significantly, averaging 2.02 days with a standard deviation of 0.94 days. Deposit transfers are also relatively infrequent. Depositors may go several months without making an interbank transfer and then move a substantial amount when they do. Because transfer activity is sporadic, we use a one-year rolling average of lagged transfer delays in our subsequent analysis to capture the payment frictions faced by each depositor over time. Another factor that may contribute to active deposit management is mental accounting. Gelman and Roussanov (2024) show that individuals temporarily increase consumption after receiving a new payment card. Consistent with this idea, Appendix Figure A-3 shows that depositors often use different bank accounts for different purposes, creating a need to move funds across their own accounts. In our sample, the mean Digital Payment Ratio is 32%, and 65% of depositors use fast payment applications. The average deposit balance is $24,774.50 with a standard deviation of $59,139.49. The mean interest rate offered on deposits is 0.09%, with a rate dispersion of 0.13%, reflecting differences in interest rates across different bank accounts. Finally, Consumption Volatility has a mean of $3,293.28, indicating variability in monthly consumption expenditures. Consumption Smoothing Efficiency has a mean of 2.73, suggesting that, on average, depositors maintain a relatively stable level of consumption relative to fluctuations in income. The variables in the table have been winsorized at the 1% level to account for outliers, including Transfer Fees , Transfer Delay , Salary , Mean Interest Rate , Consumption Volatility , Consumption Smoothing Efficiency , and Deposit Balance .
9

2.3. County-level data We use the FDIC’s annual Summary of Deposits (SOD) from 2013 to 2021, which reports each bank branch’s total deposits, parent bank (RSSDID), and county as of June 30 of the year for FDIC-insured institutions. We use SOD to construct variables relating to the deposit market concentration of U.S. banks in counties. We also query the annual American Community Survey (ACS) data for county characteristics to capture dimensions such as population, income, education, age, and digital adoption. Table 2 provides summary statistics for these characteristics, which we describe in detail below.
2.4. Zelle adoption data We retrieve all of Zelle’s partner banks from historical snapshots of their official webpage on the Wayback Machine, from which we infer monthly bank-level adoption dates. For each bank, we carefully match these Zelle partners to identifiers (RSSD IDs) using the Federal Financial Institutions Examination Council (FFIEC) data, which we use to merge with the SOD data. Figure 2 plots the cumulative number of Zelle partners over time; results are consistent with those of Balyuk and Williams (2021).
3. Interbank Transfers: Motivating Facts and Measurement
3.1. Many depositors hold meaningful balances in more than one account A first stylized fact in our data is that retail depositors commonly maintain multiple bank accounts with meaningful balances. Figure 3 shows that the vast majority of depositors hold more than one bank (and credit-card-linked) account, consistent with survey evidence that Americans maintain several financial accounts (Reville 2019). Importantly, these additional accounts are not small. For more than three quarters of depositors, the second bank account carries a sizable balance. Table 3 shows that the mean (median) balance in the largest account is $33,159 ($7,256); in the second-largest account it is $17,019 ($3,425); and in the third-largest account it is $7,548 ($1,699). 1 These balance patterns imply that depositors hold liquidity in more than one place. As a result,
1 This statistic is not directly comparable to Figure 3, which plots the distribution of all accounts in the sample including those without balance information.
10
shifting funds across accounts can involve large dollar amounts and can plausibly matter for both household payment management and bank funding.
3.2. Account specialization creates demand for transfers across a depositor’s accounts Holding multiple accounts does not by itself imply that depositors need to move funds across them. In the data, however, different accounts are often used for different purposes. Salary income may arrive in one account, while mortgage payments, credit-card payments, cash withdrawals, or investment-related transactions are made from another. These differences may reflect direct-deposit arrangements, billing relationships, ATM access, rewards, or links to brokerage accounts. 2 When income and payments are spread across accounts, depositors may need to transfer funds between them. If the accounts are at different banks, these transfers generate interbank deposit turnover. We document this pattern by aggregating transactions to the depositor–account level. For each depositor, we define the salary account as the account receiving the largest dollar amount of salary or regular-income deposits. For each payment category—loan payments, mortgage payments, credit-card payments, ATM withdrawals, check payments, and investment/brokerage payments—we define the primary account as the account with the largest dollar amount in that category. Among depositors with both salary income and activity in a given category, we report the share whose primary account differs from the salary account and the share of category spending that occurs on non-salary accounts. Figure 4 shows that 15%–24% of depositors use a different primary account for these activities than for salary income. The shares range from 15.2% for credit-card payments to 24.0% for ATM withdrawals. The differences are also sizable in dollar terms. About one quarter of credit-card, investment, check, and loan-payment dollars occur on non-salary accounts, while the corresponding shares are 38.8% for mortgage payments and 49.1% for ATM withdrawals. Appendix Section B.3 and Figure A-3 show a similar pattern within accounts: 57% of accounts have one transaction category accounting for more than half of dollar activity, and more than 90% of multi-account depositors have at least one such account. These patterns suggest that depositors do not use their accounts interchangeably. Instead,
2 We are agnostic about why depositors hold multiple bank accounts. Rewards programs, co-branded credit cards, and employer-bank relationships are possible reasons.
11
different inflows and payments are often tied to different accounts, creating a reason to move funds across banks and making transfer speed relevant for deposit management.
3.3. A new measure of how much depositors move across banks: Deposit turnover Motivated by these two stylized facts, we introduce a new depositor-level measure, deposit turnover , to summarize how actively a depositor moves funds across banks. Deposit turnover is the gross dollar volume transferred between accounts held at different depository institutions within a period. It is the depositor-level analogue of bank-level payment volume (e.g., Fedwire), and it is closely related to liquidity management and payment risk (Li, Li, and Sun 2022, Goldstein, Yang, and Zeng 2023, Li and Li 2024).
3 Ideally, we would directly link the outflow and inflow legs of the same transfer across accounts. However, our transaction data do not provide a unique identifier linking a debit in one account to the corresponding credit in another account, and consistent institution identifiers are not available across accounts. We therefore construct the transfer sample in two stages. First, we identify candidate debit–credit pairs across accounts held by the same depositor based on posting dates and transaction amounts. At this candidate-matching stage, we retain debit–credit pairs posted within the matching window and with absolute amount differences no larger than $50, including same-day, same-amount pairs. Table 4 describes this pre-screening sample and therefore includes a large number of zero-delay observations. Second, we screen candidate pairs to construct the interbank sample used in the main analysis. Exact same-day, same-amount matches without a fast-payment marker are classified as likely intrabank transfers and excluded, while same-day matches carrying a fast-payment marker remain in the interbank sample. Specifically, we developed a straightforward algorithm. On any given day t , we start by examining all debit transactions—these include transfers out and ATM or cash withdrawals—from every account that depositor i holds, which constitute approximately 20% of all transactions. For each debit transaction on day t , we search for a matching credit in another account held by the same depositor that occurs on the same day or within the following five days, from day t through day t + 5 .
3 Relatedly, gross outflows to other banks can be interpreted as realized “maturity” of deposits. Models that treat deposits as debt with random maturity imply that larger gross maturities within a period increase rollover and liquidity risk (e.g., Jermann and Xiang 2023, Bolton, Li, Wang, and Yang 2025).

After generating the candidate pairs, we move to screen interbank transfers. Same-day pairs carrying a fast-payment marker are retained. This metric captures the gross volume of interbank deposit transfers for each depositor, analogous to the gross volume reported at the bank level in Fedwire, capturing the gross payment flow of funds across banks. Because transaction descriptions are masked, we cannot use unrestricted transaction text to distinguish unmarked fee-free interbank fast payments from intrabank transfers. The baseline screen is therefore conservative: it may exclude some genuine same-day interbank transfers, but it prevents the large mass of likely intrabank transfers from entering the interbank delay measure. Additionally, it is worth noting that our measure captures the depositor-facing posting delay of matched deposit transfer pairs across banks, rather than a direct observation of true settlement time. This measure is the relevant friction for our economic mechanism: what matters for household

The focus on own-account transfers is a deliberate use of the linked structure of the data. As noted above, no field in the data links a debit directly to its corresponding credit, so both legs of a transfer must be matched on posting date and amount. The persistent depositor identifier is what makes that matching credible: it restricts the set of candidate counterparts to the small number of accounts held by the same person, so a debit–credit pair with sufficiently close posting dates and amounts within that set is less likely to be coincidental. Extending the same rule to transfers between different people would require both the sender and the receiver to appear in the sample, and would search for matches over a candidate set the size of the entire panel rather than a handful of commonly owned accounts. At that scale, amount-and-date matching would generate a large volume of false pairs and a correspondingly unreliable delay measure. Restricting the baseline measure to accounts held by the same depositor therefore improves measurement and exploits a distinctive strength of the data. We note that this scope of focusing on own-account transfers does not imply that person-to- person payments are unimportant. Transfers to other people can generate the same basic liquidity- management problem whenever outgoing funds are committed before incoming funds become available. We interpret our matched own-account transfers as the setting in which depositor- facing debit-to-credit posting delay and gross reallocation can be measured most reliably, and the Zelle exposure exercise provides complementary evidence from a technology used more broadly for person-to-person payments. Any extrapolation from own-account transfers to across-person payments is therefore an economic extension of the mechanism, not a claim that the latter are directly observed in our turnover measure. During the sample period, ACH transfers account for the majority of interbank deposit turnover. The types of interbank transfers are important because different types of transfers vary significantly in their transfer speeds. While ACH transfers can experience long delays, wire transfers and transfers initiated through fast payment applications are typically processed within a business day with minimal to no delay. Using the meta information and transfer delays for paired deposit transactions, we further report deposit turnover based on the method of transfer used. In the following analysis, we do not consider transfers that are initiated and credited within the same bank; 14
instead, the analysis below focuses on interbank transfers, and we summarize the main categories of deposit transfer across banks in Figure 5. In addition to the dollar volume of deposit turnover, which is crucial for bank funding, we present an additional set of empirical results using scaled variables. Depositors vary in their wealth; a $1,000 transfer constitutes different proportions for individuals with $1 million compared to those with $2,000 in deposits. We scale deposit turnover and other depositor-level metrics by each individual’s average monthly spending in the preceding year and report the distribution of scaled deposit turnover in both raw and logarithmic forms in Figure A-4 in Appendix B.4. Transactions completed with fast payment services such as Zelle, PayPal, Cash App, and Venmo are classified as “Instant App Transfer” transactions. Over time, there has been a noticeable uptick in these types of transactions. Additionally, transactions with metadata that include ATM-related information (physical cash withdrawal, ATM, cash, etc.) are classified as ATM transactions. These transactions have maintained a low but steady rate of occurrence. All other deposit transfers with a non-zero transaction delay that do not fall into the ATM-related, instant-payment-application-related, or wire-transfer categories, are labeled as interbank transfers, as shown in orange in the graph. Our study does not look into the specifics of choosing wire transfers as a payment method, including the decision-making process regarding the willingness to pay for superior payment services, leaving this area open for future exploration. Appendix B.1 and Appendix Figure A-2 summarize fee differences for different payment methods of interbank transfers.
3.4. A new measure of payment convenience: Transfer delays What our measure captures. Before defining the measure formally, we clarify its scope. Our transfer delay is constructed by matching outgoing and incoming legs of paired interbank trans- fers and computing the gap between posting dates. It therefore captures the depositor’s realized experience of payment frictions on the routes they actually use, rather than the technical settle- ment window of any particular payment rail. Transfer Delays and Depositor Behavior: Empirical Evidence In this section, we first document how measured transfer delays covary with depositor activeness and account balances in the transaction data. Then we provide account-level analysis with comple- mentary evidence from comparing faster and slower accounts held by the same depositor. Finally, we show how variation generated by banks’ staggered adoption of Zelle affects aggregate deposit growth at the county level.

As interbank transfers are sporadic and transfer delay is measured using a 12-month rolling average, most identifying variation in this specification is across depositors rather than within a depositor over short horizons. As a result, specifications with depositor fixed effects leave limited independent variation in measured delay. We summarize the results in two panels in Table 5. In panel (a), we report how measured transfer delays are associated with deposit turnover and balances. In panel (b), to facilitate comparisons across depositors, we present the same relationships after scaling by each depositor’s average spending over the past year and applying a log transformation to the dependent variable. When accounting for both time fixed effects and depositor-specific controls, an additional day of transfer delay is associated with about 46 fewer dollars of deposit turnover and about 1,700 more dollars of deposit balance; in consumption units, the scaled deposit turnover is 16.4% lower and the scaled deposit balance is 5.2% higher. Table 5 documents descriptive equilibrium relationships between depositors’ realized transfer delays and their deposit-management behavior. Depositors facing longer measured delays transfer less and maintain larger balances, but these relationships combine payment frictions with persistent differences in account portfolios, digital sophistication, liquidity preferences, and rate-shopping intensity. The specifications focus on different margins. The dollar-level turnover results describe total observed transfer volume, whereas the log-scaled turnover specifications are restricted to months with positive transfers and therefore describe the intensive margin conditional on being active. Sorting and interpretation. A natural alternative interpretation of these relationships is equilib- rium sorting. Depositors with greater demand for active liquidity management may choose faster institutions, accounts, or payment rails and may also transfer more frequently. This form of sorting is economically plausible and is not inconsistent with the heterogeneity emphasized by our model: depositors with more volatile liquidity needs, stronger rate-shopping incentives, or greater digital sophistication may place a higher value on transfer speed, even though the model itself does not endogenize bank choice. Accordingly, the negative delay–turnover association in Table 5 may combine a response to payment frictions with revealed demand for faster payments. We also highlight that the positive association between delay and balances places an additional restriction on a pure sorting explanation. Sorting alone would need to imply that depositors who 18
maintain lower transactional balances systematically select faster institutions or routes, conditional on observed consumption volatility, rate dispersion, salary, digital-payment use, and common time effects. Such sorting is possible—for example, financially sophisticated depositors may both economize on idle balances and seek faster technology—but it does not follow mechanically from a high underlying demand for turnover. We therefore view Table 5 as documenting an economically meaningful equilibrium relationship rather than a treatment effect. Looking forward, the within- depositor account analysis in Table 6 removes persistent depositor type, while the Zelle exposure design in Section 4.3 provides complementary evidence based on a technology rollout. 4.2. Transfer delays, deposit movements in and out of banks, and rate sensitivity The preceding depositor-level results primarily reflect cross-sectional variation. We now provide a more demanding comparison across accounts held by the same depositor. Depositor fixed effects absorb persistent household characteristics. Specifically, we extend the baseline analysis in Table 5 and Figure 7 to account-level balance changes. These changes summarize the net inflows and outflows of each observed bank account and can reflect reallocation to other bank accounts as well as to unobserved outside destinations. This approach is useful when within-sample deposit-rate spreads are small and when relevant alternatives may include higher-yielding nonbank savings vehicles such as money market mutual funds. We highlight that, although we do not observe nonbank counterparties directly, movements into money market funds or brokerage accounts generally involve a bank-facing cash leg. Account-level balance changes can therefore capture the net consequences of transfer delays on such reallocations, even though we cannot separately measure bank-to-nonbank transfers.

Delays in those bank-facing legs can affect when funds become available and therefore the amount of liquidity that investors keep pre-positioned in transaction accounts. Our directly measured interbank delays provide evidence on this common bank-facing friction, while the account-level balance specification captures its possible net consequences. In that sense, we present this as an implication of the mechanism rather than as direct observation of bank-to-nonbank transfers.

Consistent with Table 5, among a depositor’s different transactional bank accounts, Table 6 shows that faster accounts are associated with lower balances (columns 1–2). This effect strengthens when comparative market rates are higher and when consumption volatility is higher. Specifically, faster accounts have lower balances, particularly when outside rates are high (row 2) and among depositors with above-median consumption volatility (columns 3–4). Overall, these findings are consistent with the baseline results in Table 5 and Figure 7, suggesting that depositor activeness reflects a trade-off between managing uncertain consumption needs and optimizing savings. In reality, many daily expenditures are not directly handled from bank accounts; credit cards, which on average account for around 30% of total spending, are another important payment channel for many depositors. Because credit cards act much like lines of credit and permit flexible repayment schedules, the uncertainty of any waiting period for fund transfers becomes less important (Akerlof and Milbourne 1980). Consistent with this view, columns (5) and (6) in Table 6 suggest that accounts experiencing more credit card usage have a weaker dampening effect of payment delays on depositors’ sensitivity to rate spreads. To sum up, accounts with shorter measured delays are associated with larger subsequent reduc- tions, or smaller increases, in their share of the depositor’s total bank deposits. Further, account-level evidence suggests depositors are more responsive to rate spreads when funds can be moved more quickly. We show quantitative results consistent with these reduced-form observations in Section 6 using a calibrated model that incorporates these trade-offs.

Taken together, the county-level results provide aggregate evidence consistent with the depositor- level mechanism. Counties more exposed to banks adopting Zelle experience shorter measured transfer delays and slower deposit growth, which is the pattern predicted by a mechanism in which faster payments reduce the need to keep funds pre-positioned in transactional accounts. They complement the micro evidence and motivate the model by showing that payment-technology adoption is associated with deposit dynamics in the expected direction.
5. A Model of Deposit Demand with Transfer Delays
To reconcile our empirical findings and further quantify the impact of payment convenience on banks’ deposit balances and depositor activity, in this section we develop a new deposit management 24
model in the spirit of Alvarez and Lippi (2009) and Kaplan and Violante (2014), incorporating both transfer delays and consumption volatility. The model illustrates how payment convenience emerges from both the transactional function of money, showing that shorter transfer delays allow depositors to maintain lower balances in low-interest deposit accounts while increasing deposit transfers. Our key theoretical contribution is the explicit incorporation of uncertain transfer delays, an important factor omitted in existing liquidity management models. Our model predictions align closely with our empirical analysis in Section 4. In Section 6, we further calibrate the model and conduct counterfactual analyses to evaluate the effects of faster payment technologies on banking and monetary policy. Time is modeled as continuous. A representative depositor with discount rate β is endowed with two bank accounts, account C and account S , which are offered by different banks, starting at time t = 0 . Motivated by the evidence of account specialization discussed earlier, and without loss of generality, we assume that deposits in bank account C are non-interest-bearing yet are used by the depositor for spending and to pay interest-bearing liabilities such as credit card debts and mortgages, while deposits in bank account S are interest-bearing with an exogenous interest rate of r > 0 . As in Alvarez and Lippi (2009), suppose the average net consumption (including debt repayment) outflow is exogenous: let g > 0 denote its constant mean rate from bank account C . Different from their setup, we further assume that the net consumption flow c (total spending minus income) follows a Brownian motion, dc = − gdt + σdw , where w is a standard Wiener process, and g > 0 and σ > 0 are the drift and volatility, respectively. Additionally, denote by m the balance of bank account C , which, as we will show, is a crucial state variable in the model. It is important to note that the assumption of account C being non-interest-bearing is not critical. What is essential is that the two accounts offer different interest rates, and we hence also refer to r as the interest rate spread in this simple two-account model. To model deposit turnover and its determinants, we assume that the depositor can transfer funds between the two bank accounts in either direction: from account C to account S or vice versa. Importantly, to account for payment and transfer delays, as previously discussed, we assume that once an outgoing payment is initiated from one bank account, the corresponding incoming payment to the other account is processed only after a delay, modeled by an independent Poisson process with rate κ . Importantly, these deposits in transit can neither earn interest nor be used to meet 25
spending needs, including any repayments of liabilities. This captures the potential losses due to delays in deposit transfers. Additionally, we assume that when m = 0 , meaning bank account C has a zero balance, a deposit transfer from bank account S to account C incurs no delays but does involve a penalty b > 0 , irrespective of the transfer size. This penalty can be interpreted as the total costs associated with payday borrowing, overdrafting, or any mental cost of lack of liquidity. Technically, this assumption also aids in tractability by ruling out defaults and ensuring non-negativity of account balances in bank account C . This helps introduce a straightforward boundary condition, as we will specify below. Notably, however, in our model, the balance of bank account S is not required to be non-negative, capturing potential borrowing or shorting positions. Propositions 1 and 2 organize the central patterns in the reduced-form evidence. Table 5 shows that depositors facing longer measured delays transfer less and maintain larger balances. Table 6 shows that, within a depositor, accounts with shorter measured delays subsequently experience larger balance-share reductions. Table 8 shows that greater exposure to fast-payment adoption predicts both shorter measured delays and slower county deposit growth. These signs all match the model’s direct payment-speed predictions. The heterogeneity evidence is also qualitatively consistent with the model’s precautionary chan- nel. Figure 7 and the above-median-volatility specifications in Table 6 indicate stronger responses among depositors with greater consumption uncertainty. Because those empirical outcomes are expressed as log-scaled semi-elasticities or balance shares, whereas the model’s amplification result 28
is stated in dollar levels, we interpret this evidence as directional support rather than as a direct estimate of the model’s cross-partials. The intuition for Proposition 1 is straightforward. Faster transfers reduce the amount of liquidity that must be pre-positioned in the low-interest account C , while a higher interest rate spread raises the opportunity cost of holding that liquidity. Depositors with greater consumption volatility maintain larger precautionary balances. Under the proportional shortfall-cost specification b = qσ , the entire target policy scales with σ , so the dollar balance reduction produced by faster transfers is larger for higher- σ depositors. For Proposition 2, greater transfer efficiency has two opposing effects. Transfers complete more frequently, but the balance has less time to move away from its target before completion, reducing average transfer size. In the region of n ≥ 3 , the frequency effect dominates, so completed transfer volume rises with κ . Because turnover also scales with σ when q is held fixed, higher- σ depositors experience larger dollar increases in turnover. As another benchmark to understand the model mechanisms, we consider the limiting case where κ → ∞ , so that the expected transfer delay approaches zero and transfers between the two accounts become instantaneous. In this scenario, the model reduces to a special case of the Alvarez and Lippi (2009) model, characterized by zero transfer fees and the constant opportunity to freely transfer funds. Returning to our general setting with finite delays, greater consumption uncertainty raises the value of liquidity in account C , raises target balances, widens the inaction region in proportion 29
to σ , and increases completed voluntary transfer volume in dollar terms (Kaplan and Violante 2014). A greater interest rate spread makes account S a more attractive store of value and lowers both target balances. At a fixed transfer technology, it also reduces completed voluntary turnover in the limiting solution. It is also useful to compare our solution to the standard Baumol-Tobin model, where inaction in transactions is driven by transaction costs, or equivalently, transfer fees in the context of deposits. To highlight the novel aspect of transfer delays, as documented in Sections 2 and 3, we explicitly model delays in deposit transfers while abstracting away from transfer fees. There are fundamental differences between transfer delays and transfer fees.
